items.content: There is an explanation in the handbook in Section 2 to help you remember the diagram.
You can describe behaviour in a conversation using a simple sense and respond model.
Think of it as a snapshot of what's happening for someone in a conversation.
Point to each circle as you explain:
[I see/hear] We take in information from the outside world through our senses. Seeing and hearing are the main senses we use in conversations.

[I think/feel] We process that information internally. Our mood or physical needs can influence how we do that because we also use data from our bodies.
Thinking processes include:

- What we pay attention to
- The meaning we make from things and the language we use
- The assumptions that we hold as true
- Reasoning and how we make judgements or inferences about things
[I say/do] We act on our thoughts or feelings. Often unconsciously reacting, sometimes consciously responding.
We are going to look at assumptions first and then how feelings can influence assumptions.
Prepare BORs in 2/3s for **8 minutes** if not already done

items.content: We are going to demonstrate how easily and how quickly we can make assumptions.
You’ll need your pen and paper for this.
Facilitator to group:
I’m going to ask [Producer/Co-facilitator] to pick an object in their space that we can’t see and tell me what that object is briefly…
Facilitator to Producer/Co-facilitator
[Producer/Co-facilitator], What object are you looking at?
Producer/Co-facilitator:
I can see a plant.
Facilitator to group:
Think about what happened for the rest of you when you heard [Producer/Co-facilitator] say that?
What are you imagining about that plant? What are you assuming about that plant?
Whatever you’re thinking or imagining about that plant, draw that on your paper, adding as much or as little detail as you’d like.
Pause for drawing
Everyone, please hold up your paper to the camera so we can see what you think this plant is like.
Now I am going to use some questions to check the assumptions I have about that plant.
Facilitator to Producer/Co-facilitator:
[Producer/Co-facilitator], may I ask:
What kind of plant is it?
Whereabouts is that plant?
And is there anything else about that plant?
And now, please could you all add some more detail to your pictures and show them to the camera.
Pause for sharing
What happened for you after you had more information about the plant?
Facilitate short discussion
Now let’s find out what this plant is…
Producer/Co-facilitator shows the plant.
Facilitator to group:
How accurate was your drawing or description?
On a scale of 1-5, where 1 is least accurate, and 5 is super accurate, let’s see a show of fingers as to how accurate your assumptions were about [Producer/Co-facilitator]’s plant.
Acknowledge what people score themselves at.
Participate in demo if no co-facilitator

items.content: You will have **8 minutes** to do this exercise in breakout rooms.
You will work in pairs or threes, with one person as the Chooser and the other(s) as the Asker(s).  You’re going to do what we just did.
The exercise is going in the chat so it should travel to the breakout room with you. If you are on a mobile device, you might want to take a note of it in case you can’t see it.
The Chooser picks an object they can see but the Asker(s) can’t and says “I can see a ___” without showing the object.
The Asker(s) draws their version of the object on a piece of paper, then shows it to the Chooser.

The Asker(s) asks just two or three of these questions of the Chooser about the object:
- What kind of ___?
- Whereabouts is ___?
- Is there anything else about ___?
The Asker(s) updates their drawings based on the Chooser’s answers, then shows them to the Chooser again.
The Chooser reveals the object and compares it with the Asker(s)’ drawings.
Manage the time so everyone gets a chance to ask the questions
Remember – this not about guessing the object, it’s about assumptions!
When you come back, we’ll find out what you noticed about making assumptions.
Any questions before we send you in?

resources.description: Use assumptions diagram to explain how feelings affect assumptions

blocks.handover_comment: to talk about assumptions and feelings breakout activity.

items.content: The reason we do this exercise is to show how easily and quickly we make assumptions. They may be right or wrong. They can change when we have new information.
We can easily verify whether we are right or wrong talking about a physical object.
It’s harder with abstract concepts like trust, fairness, justice and so on – this is where many misunderstanding occur between people.
The questions we suggested: What kind of? Whereabouts? Anything else? are useful to test assumptions.
Let’s now think about how our feelings affect our assumptions.
Point to the middle step on the assumptions model
By feelings, I also mean sensations, emotions, and mood.
Our thinking processes are entwined with our feelings – we could say our thoughts are always coloured by our feelings.
This is why we use the traffic light model - red/amber(yellow)/green - on the middle step which is “I think/feel”
Shade the “I think/feel step” on the diagram with red/orange/green pens (or use red/yellow/green Post-its or transparent sheets) to show what you mean.
Different emotions or feelings can affect our thinking differently.
For example, when we are in red, we might be more likely to perceive threat and act quickly.
When in green, we may be more creative in our thinking.

Learners will be able to:

- Explain how assumptions affect conversations
- Describe the link between state and assumptions

Suggested learning outcomes for further trainings/interventions

- Discuss where their own assumptions come from
- Describe limiting and helpful assumptions they hold
- Explain how assumptions might lead to stereotyping and prejudice
